          # legacy `permission` field collapses the granular roles onto
          # admin/write/read/none, "where the maintain role is mapped to write
          # and the triage role is mapped to read" — which is exactly the
          # predicate wanted here: write + maintain + admin pass, triage and
          # read do not. It also resolves a CUSTOM repository role to its base
          # role, whereas `role_name` returns the custom role's own name and
          # would silently drop such a contributor to untrusted. (Custom roles
          # are not available on this org's current plan, so that part is
          # future-proofing.) role_name is still logged, for diagnosis.
          # Returns 0 = has write, 1 = resolved and does NOT have write,
          # 2 = COULD NOT RESOLVE. The third case used to collapse into the
          # second, which is not a safe default here: `trusted=false` makes
          # every consumer SKIP, and GitHub reports a skipped required job as
          # Success — so one 502 or secondary rate limit turned a trusted PR
          # into zero CI that renders green, with the only evidence a warning
          # inside a job whose conclusion is Success. Failing closed has to
          # mean this job FAILS, leaving a red check, not that its consumers
          # quietly stand down. The caller turns a 2 into exit 1.
          has_write() {
            local user="$1" out err perm role
            # stderr to a FILE, not 2>&1 into `out`: a diagnostic on a
            # SUCCESSFUL call would otherwise land in the string being parsed
            # below, and the first token of a warning is not a permission.
            err=$(mktemp)
            # One request, both fields. Fetching them in two calls doubled the
            # requests per principal for a log line.
            if ! out=$(gh api "repos/${REPO}/collaborators/${user}/permission" --jq '"\(.permission) \(.role_name)"' 2>"$err"); then

The API said: $(tr '\n' ' ' < "$err"). If the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN is not accepted by this endpoint, set a CI_TRUST_TOKEN repository secret (Metadata: read) — every caller already forwards it to this workflow as trust_token." >&2
              rm -f "$err"
              return 2
            fi
            rm -f "$err"
            perm="${out%% *}"
            role="${out#* }"
            echo "  ${user}: permission=${perm} (role_name=${role})"

              admin | write) return 0 ;;
              *) return 1 ;;

          # trusts every event that is not literally that one — and the set of
          # "every other event" is not the two this reasoning covers. Adding
          # `pull_request:` back to a caller (which lint.yml's trigger comment
          # used to invite), or an issue_comment / workflow_run /
          # pull_request_review_comment trigger, would arrive under a
          # different name, take the trusted branch with zero principal checks
          # and zero API calls, and run fork-supplied code on the self-hosted
          # pool. Anything not named below is refused.

            reason="event '${EVENT_NAME}' is not an allow-listed trigger for the self-hosted lanes; add it to the case above deliberately if it should be"

            # person; dedupe so the common case is one API call.
            # The owner check exists because whoever owns a fork controls who
            # may push to it. That reasoning only holds for a PERSONAL fork:
            # for an org-owned one the owner is an org, "write access for an
            # organization" is not a thing this endpoint can answer, and the
            # equivalent question (who in that org can push) is not visible to
            # us at all. So for org-owned forks the owner is dropped from the
            # principal list and the PR author plus the sender carry it.
            #
            # The residual risk is the same shape as the one already accepted
            # for personal forks: another principal with push access to the
            # fork can merge code that runs here, just with a larger set
            # behind it. Worth knowing when adding org-owned forks.
            #
            # The PR AUTHOR is always a principal, and on an org-owned fork it
            # is the only one tied to the code. `sender` is the pusher on
            # `synchronize`, but on `reopened`, `labeled` and `unlabeled` it is
            # whoever performed that action, which is normally a maintainer.
            # Without the author, a maintainer adding the `preview` label to a
            # PR from a throwaway org-owned fork would resolve the gate against
            # the maintainer's own write access and run fork code here with no
            # check on who supplied it. Personal forks were already covered by
            # the head-owner check; this closes the org-owned path.
            principals=()
            [[ -n "${PR_AUTHOR:-}" ]] && principals+=("$PR_AUTHOR")
            if [[ "$HEAD_OWNER_TYPE" == "Organization" ]]; then
              echo "note: head repo is org-owned (${HEAD_OWNER}); checking the PR author and the sender"
            elif [[ -n "${HEAD_OWNER:-}" && "$HEAD_OWNER" != "${PR_AUTHOR:-}" ]]; then

              done

            fi

              reason="no identifiable principal on this fork PR"

              echo "needs_approval=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
              echo "::notice title=Untrusted ref::${reason}"

            trusted=true
            reason="every identifiable principal on this fork PR has write on ${REPO}"

              # `|| rc=$?` rather than `if ! has_write`: this needs the
              # DISTINCTION between 1 and 2, and it must not trip `set -e`.

                # fail the gate so the required checks downstream go RED and a
                # human looks, rather than skipping green.
                exit 1
              fi
              if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then
                trusted=false
                # Resolved and lacks write: the one untrusted outcome a
                # ci-approval reviewer may override for this run.
                needs_approval=true
                reason="'${u}' does not have write access to ${REPO}"
                break
              fi
            done
          fi

          echo "trusted=${trusted}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "needs_approval=${needs_approval:-false}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "reason=${reason}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

          if [[ "$trusted" == "true" ]]; then
            echo "::notice title=Trusted::${reason}"
          elif [[ "${needs_approval:-false}" == "true" ]]; then
            echo "::notice title=Awaiting approval::${reason}. A ci-approval reviewer can approve this run (Review deployments on the PR); regular contributors belong in the pawtograder-contributors team instead."
          else
            echo "::notice title=Untrusted ref::${reason}. Self-hosted lanes (lint, unit tests, E2E, preview) are skipped."
          fi

        name: Apply label requirement
        # Whether this run is WANTED (label present, or not required), worked

        # approval job asks a reviewer only for runs that are wanted, so an

          # for why this is full_name rather than the `fork` flag.

          set -euo pipefail

            echo "wanted=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            exit 0
          fi

          # Same-repo PRs are exempt from the label. The label exists so that
          # a preview namespace is never created for code we have not decided
          # to run — which is a question about FORKS. A branch in this repo
          # could only be pushed by someone who already holds write, and those
          # PRs had automatic previews before the trust gate existed; making
          # them opt-in was a side effect of the label, not a decision anyone
          # took. `HEAD_REPO` is the positive `full_name` test, not
          # `head.repo.fork != true`, which reads empty (and so "same repo")
          # when the head repository metadata is absent.
          #
          # Consequence worth knowing: on a same-repo PR, removing the
          # `preview` label tears the namespace down (preview.yml maps
          # `unlabeled` to destroy) but the next push redeploys it, because

            echo "::notice title=Preview approved::head branch lives in ${REPO}, so the '${REQUIRE_LABEL}' label is not required"
            exit 0
          fi

          # Everything past here is a fork PR (or one whose head repo is gone).
          if [[ "$FORKS_ALLOWED" != "true" ]]; then
            echo "wanted=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
